title: US Army to detonate tonnes of unstable explosives in Iowa despite court order
summary: The Army says "swift action" is necessary to protect its personnel and nearby communities around its ammunition plant in Iowa.
text:
US Army to detonate tonnes of unstable explosives in Iowa despite court order
- Published
The US Army plans to move ahead with detonating five tonnes of degraded explosives in Iowa despite a ruling to halt it indefinitely, a new court filing shows.
"To protect its personnel and the surrounding communities, the Army needs to take swift action," the justice department notified the court on Saturday. "Protection of human health and the environment demand action now, not delay."
The court had ordered a pause after environmental groups sued to stop the detonation, arguing the army failed to consider safer alternatives.
The detonation was originally scheduled for Friday at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown. The army now plans to act by 24 November under an emergency exemption.
In the new filing, the Department of the Army argued that a controlled detonation was necessary to protect the public from an unplanned explosion, a risk it said would become more likely as temperatures were set to fall in the coming days.
"There is an immediate risk that the lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant will explode as temperatures are expected to drop below 30 degrees Fahrenheit (-1C) in the next several days," the filing states.
It argued that the army had removed the doors to the bunker where the barrels were stored in preparation for the detonation and that made the explosives more "vulnerable to temperature changes".
The government has not released details for the rescheduled detonation.
Earlier, the army had warned residents to leave their homes for six hours on the original scheduled day of the explosion, for the duration of the explosion and until the dust settled. An advisory warned "all humans" to avoid being outside in the affected areas while the demolition detonation was set to take place.
Lead azide is a highly volatile compound used as a detonator. Earlier this year, the IAAAP found that the material had degraded over time to the point where it was now too risky to move the material, according to Iowa Public Radio.
On Friday, the military said it was working with the Department of Health and Human Services and the EPA to ensure the explosion was done in the safest manner possible.
Military and environmental officials determined that detonating it in place was the safest way to eliminate the explosive safety hazard.
The EPA, which granted an emergency permit to detonate 68 drums of the material, said it did so because the explosion risk "presented an imminent and substantial threat to human health and the environment".
One of the Environmental groups suing to pause the detonation, the Iowa Environmental Council, argued that many Iowans living within the risk-zone were unaware that the explosion was scheduled to happen.
"There is no safe level of lead exposure, and Iowans were given just days to prepare for the November 20 detonation," the organisation said in a press statement.

title: 'Danger seems greater all the time': Ukrainians search for missing after Russian strikes
summary: The BBC's Sarah Rainsford reports from the scene of a collapsed residential building in Ukraine's Kyiv region.
text:
'Danger seems greater all the time': Ukrainians search for missing after Russian strikes
At least three bodies have been recovered the site of a residential building that was hit by a Russian strike in the Kyiv region, Ukraine's State Emergency Services said.
A woman in her forties and a teenage boy have so far been identified as rescue workers continue to search the rubble for those who are still trapped.
Continued warnings of further drone threats near the site are hampering efforts, the service added, but some people were successfully evacuated earlier in the day.
"We are living a nightmare... only God knows when it will end," one woman told the BBC's Sarah Rainsford, who's reporting from Ukraine's Kyiv region.

title: Lebanese villagers return to wrecked homes as the Israeli army pulls back
summary: In a pilot project in a village in southern Lebanon, Israeli forces have left and the Lebanese army moved it. But villagers who return find their houses wrecked.
text:
Lebanese villagers return to wrecked homes as the Israeli army pulls back
ZAWTAR AL-GHARBIYAH, Lebanon — After two decades of working installing vehicle air conditioning in Saudi Arabia, Atef Kadouh saved up enough money to build a house in his hometown in southern Lebanon.
He and his wife, Soumaya Yaghi lived in the house for 40 years and had five children — all born at home.
Now there are four.
A photo of the youngest, Adel, is propped up in a basket of dried flowers near the doorway.
Adel, clean-cut with a trimmed beard, was a sports teacher and a basketball champion who was planning to travel to France this summer to pursue his doctorate. When the war with Israel began this year, he decided to volunteer as an ambulance driver.
The Israeli military killed him and four other medics on March 28 in a drone strike as the first responders buried a 75-year-old man who had died in hospital.
"This one broke me," his father says. "He was my youngest son, 27 years old. There have been wars in every country in the world but there are rules for war … you attack a paramedic rescuing wounded people, children? He was not a fighter at the front."
He says he warned his son that Israel could not be trusted not to kill medical personnel.
"He would not listen to me. He said, 'Dad there are wounded children — we have to go rescue them,'" he says.
Lebanon's Health Ministry says Israel has killed more than 135 first responders and medical staff in the past two years.
Asked about this airstrike, the Israeli military replied, without providing proof, that militants routinely pose as paramedics and transport weapons in ambulances for the militant group Hezbollah and its allies.
It did not respond to follow-up questions pointing out the five were not killed in an ambulance but at a burial.
A test case
The Kadouh family returned to the village in July when it became the first and until now only test of a U.S.-brokered plan for Israeli forces to withdraw and the Lebanese army to take over.
The plan is aimed at keeping Iran-backed Hezbollah out of the area, after they started firing rockets across the nearby border in solidarity with the Palestinian militant group Hamas who launched a surprise attack on southern Israel in October 2023.
Israel responded with devastating air strikes and eventually a ground invasion, and says it has continued attacks in south Lebanon following a U.S.-brokered ceasefire this year to eliminate what it believes are continued threats to northern Israel. Israel's defense minister has acknowledged destroying more than 20,000 homes across the Lebanese border in a self-declared security zone.
When Kadouh and Yaghi returned to the village, they found that Israeli soldiers had occupied their house. And then it had been set on fire.
Wrecked home
Upstairs in the hallway, near scorched walls and shattered windows, what appeared to be a work roster was written on the wall in blue marker in Hebrew with the first names of Israeli soldiers.

title: Miley Cyrus marries Maxx Morando in California ceremony
summary: The couple have been together for four years and were engaged in 2025.
text:
Miley Cyrus marries Maxx Morando in California ceremony
- Published
Miley Cyrus has married her partner of four years Maxx Morando during a ceremony in Palm Springs, California.
Photos of the wedding on Saturday show the ceremony took place by a swimming pool with the pair standing under an arch covered in white flowers.
The singer's mother, Tish Cyrus, and sister, Noah Cyrus, were in attendance, Entertainment Tonight reported.
Grammy-winning Cyrus, who donned a white dress for the wedding, confirmed her engagement to the 28-year-old drummer during an interview with US TV show Good Morning America last year.
- 'Angel by my side' - Miley Cyrus pays tribute to godmother Dolly Parton 
  - Published26 August
- Miley Cyrus confirms engagement to musician Maxx Morando 
  - Published3 December 2025
She said Morando had got down on one knee for the proposal during a trip to Asia.
"I am not easy to surprise because I love to control every situation and I had completely surrendered and I'm telling you, I was so, so, so surprised," she said.
During an interview with Wonderland, Morando said he "had to be really sneaky" to keep his proposal plans a secret.
"We went to Tokyo first for a couple days, and then on to Kyoto. I think she had a sense that it was coming, so I was waiting until the very last moment of the very last day to throw her off the scent as much as I could," he said.
Cyrus, 33, had previously been married to Australian actor Liam Hemsworth but the couple separated in 2019.
The singer, whose hits include Flowers and Party in the U.S.A, married Hunger Games star Hemsworth in 2018 after the couple were in a relationship for a decade.
Speaking to British Vogue in 2023, Cyrus said she and 28-year-old Morando met after being "put on a blind date".
Morando is a drummer with LA-based band Liily. The band participated in NBC's Miley's New Year's Eve Party - hosted by Cyrus - in 2022, alongside musicians including Cyrus's late godmother Dolly Parton and David Byrne.

title: Russia-bound ship towed away after it was attacked in Gulf of Finland
summary: Finnish defence forces say that Ukraine was likely behind the drone strike on Saturday. Kyiv has yet to comment.
text:
Russia-bound ship towed away after it was attacked in Gulf of Finland
- Published
A Russian cargo vessel that was hit by a drone attack in the eastern Gulf of Finland is being towed away, authorities have said.
The the Sparta II had been bound for Russia's Baltic exclave Kaliningrad when it was hit on Saturday morning, sparking a fire aboard.
It then drifted into Finnish waters and its crew were evacuated to Russia. Finnish defence forces said Ukraine was likely behind the attack. Kyiv has yet to comment.
Finland's Border Guard said on Sunday afternoon that fire was no longer visible from the outside but thermal cameras showed that some containers on the ship were still warm.
The Sparta II was "slightly listing", Finnish authorities added, but the "situation is stable" and no fuel or other "hazardous substance leaks" had been detected.
Kaliningrad Governor Alexei Besprozvannykh said two drones appeared to have been used in the strike and that there was "no threat" to his territory's supplies.
The Sparta II was sanctioned by the US in 2022 and Ukraine earlier this year, and is run by a Russian company, according to the Ukrainian and US governments.
The company says it was established within the structure of Russia's defence ministry in 2011 and since 2015 has been operating within the military construction complex.
Finland's coast guard said it had been alerted to the attack at around 08:50 local time (06:50 GMT) on Saturday and that the cargo vessel had been located approximately 50km west of the island of Suursaari in the Gulf of Finland.
This prompted "temporary aviation and maritime restrictions" around the area, Finnish border officials said.
"War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity," Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said. "Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor."
Shortly after the incident, Finland's defence ministry said a Russian helicopter was suspected of violating the country's airspace, potentially linked to "rescue or tracking operations".
While Besprozvannykh initially said the crew of the Sparta II intended to repair the ship and carry on their journey, the Finnish Border Guard later said they had been evacuated to another Russian vessel that was en route to Russia.
Jukka-Pekka Lumilahti, director of maritime operations at the Finnish Border Guard, said during a news conference on Sunday that one Sparta II crew member had suffered minor injuries.
The Russian rescue vessel Murman is leading towing operations with the support of a Finnish guard ship and a Estonian naval patrol vessel.
Kaliningrad is a Russian exclave that sits between Poland and Lithuania.
Finnish Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen said that the Border Guard was responsible for the investigation into the attack and was co-operating with other relevant authorities.
Nato has also been informed, the defence ministry said.

title: Meet the young authors! A literacy program inspires kids in South Africa
summary: South Africa is working to overcome a children's literacy crisis. In one Johannesburg township, a reading club is instilling a love of books in kids — and inspiring them to become authors.
text:
Meet the young authors! A literacy program inspires kids in South Africa
JOHANNESBURG — It's an ordinary Saturday morning in Alexandra township, known simply as Alex or sometimes dubbed Gomora, a reference to the biblical city of Gomorrah that was known for its wickedness.
That nickname stems from Alexandra's high crime rates. It's a high-density area, where tin shacks stretch as far as the eye can see and rotting garbage piles up along potholed streets.
But that image doesn't intrude on an event at a small building at the Kwabhekilanga Sports Ground. There's a palpable sense of excitement. Something different is happening this weekend and community members have turned up for it.
It's a book launch for a collection entitled From Gomora to the World. Stories from Alex. The seven stories in the self-published anthology have been written by children from the township who attend a free weekly literacy program.
South Africa is in the midst of a literacy crisis, with one international study showing a majority of 10-year-olds — some 81% — are unable to read for meaning in any of South Africa's 12 official languages.
The grassroots program Read Alex has been trying to change this, offering a weekend reading club, mainly in English, to instill a love of books in children. Launched by the Run Alex Athletics Club, it has about 50 participants. Among the activities: an annual public speaking competition, two spelling bees and a book drive on Mandela Day every year that brings in about 500 volumes — some of which the kids take home and some of which go to libraries.
Now, not only are the children getting to practice their reading, some of them have tried their hand at writing their own stories.
The newly published authors sit up front, ready to sign the pile of freshly-printed books for sale and answer questions about their process.
Thirteen-year-old Fiona Mogane, the bespectacled author of "Lindani's Modelling Journey," is one of them.
"It's about a girl who discovered a lot of challenges throughout her journey," Fiona explains. One of those challenges is that the main character Lindani's mother is an alcoholic, spending what little money the family has on drink — including government grant money meant for her daughter's welfare. She also shouts at her daughter a lot, and sometimes Lindani worries she will follow in her mother's footsteps.
Fiona writes: "Sometimes a thought intrudes on Lindani's mind, telling her that if she took some alcohol, it would make her feel better and stand up for herself …. However Lindani always pulls herself out of that thought: she knows she is stronger than that."
Phelelisa Somana, one of the coordinators of the book project, says she was impressed with the maturity of Fiona's story.
"When I read her story it had a very deep theme that I didn't expect a child to delve into in a way that she did," says Somana.

title: Lock of former US President George Washington's hair sells for $4,000
summary: The hair was given as a sign of friendship shortly before Washington's death in 1799, according to a descendent of its former owner.
text:
Lock of former US President George Washington's hair sells for $4,000
- Published
A framed lock of hair from America's first president, George Washington, has been sold at auction for $4,000 (£3,058).
The hair once belonged to John Gadsby, who entertained Washington in 1799 just before the latter's death the same year, and was later obtained by a collector called John K Lattimer from a descendent of Gadsby's, according to Richmond Auctions, which sold the item.
Its new owner has not been named.
Saturday's sale is not the most expensive for Washington hair at auction. Three strands thought to have been removed from him close to or after his death stored in a locket sold for nearly $40,000 in 2021.
Gadsby, a resident of what in 1799 was the town of Alexandria in Virginia, entertained Washington for dinner shortly before his death later that year, according to a testament given in 1928 by Gadsby's granddaughter, Julia Ten Eyck McBlair, and which was posted on the Richmond Auctions website.
McBlair stated that her grandfather came into possession of Washington's hair "in view of the friendship and association with his last days" and had it framed and hung "under General Washington's portrait in our home in Washington City, there I have seen it all my life".
Gadsby hosted Washington's two birthday celebrations in 1798 and 1799, Richmond Auctions states.
Washington led American forces to victory against the British in the War of Independence and helped draft the US Constitution before becoming the country's first president in 1788. He stepped down in 1797 after serving two terms.
Several locks of Washington's hair have been preserved, including at least 50 examples that are in a collection at his former residence, Mount Vernon, which is now a museum.
"Public displays of hair from friends or loved ones peaked in the 19th century, but had long been popular among affluent families like the Washingtons," a blog on the Mount Vernon website states.
As well as lockets of his hair, other items associated with Washington have also done well at auction.
In July, a signed letter by Washington from 1776, in which he asks for soldiers for the Continental Army to fight the British, sold for $109,800.

title: Explosion on Russian ship at Libya port caused by suspected drone attack, officials say
summary: Libya's eastern government says the ship had stopped for fuel and supplies on its way back to Russia.
text:
Explosion on Russian ship at Libya port caused by suspected drone attack, officials say
- Published
An explosion on a Russian ship docked at Benghazi naval base port was caused by a suspected drone attack, Libya's eastern government has said.
The explosion happened at dawn on Sunday, while the ship had stopped for fuel and supplies on its way back to Russia, Libyan state media reported, citing the eastern government.
It added that the site was secured, and there were no casualties. Moscow has yet to comment.
Satellite imagery from Planet Labs PBC, reviewed by BBC Verify, shows a boat on fire at 0547 GMT at the Benghazi port, with a separate image captured several hours later appearing to show the same vessel partially submerged.
Videos posted on social media and geolocated by BBC Verify show the ship engulfed in flames and smoke, while it is still dark.
The eastern-based Government of National Stability (GNS) said the Russian ship was using the Benghazi port within the framework of an existing maritime agreement.
Sunday's incident is under investigation, and authorities are coordinating with their Russian counterparts to determine the source of the suspected attack and who is responsible for it, GNS added.
GNS condemned the attack on a ship inside a Libyan port, and called it a violation of maritime safety and an attack on their sovereignty. It said Libya was not party to the Russia-Ukraine war, or any other conflict beyond its borders.
Separately, Libya's internationally recognised government in Tripoli - the Government of National Unity (GNU) - warned against hosting foreign forces and allowing them to use facilities in a statement published by state media.
GNU said such activity raises "serious fears" about "risks that may result from involving ports and civilian facilities in activities related to external conflicts, and the resulting threat to the lives of citizens and the safety of national facilities and assets".
Libya fractured into violence and instability after its leader Muammar Gaddafi was overthrown in 2011, leading to the opposing governments.
Benghazi is more than 2,000 km (1,243 miles) away from the Russian capital Moscow.
  - Published1 hour ago

title: Climate change talks fall apart in final hours over fossil fuels
summary: Some 200 countries gathered in Antalya, Turkey, for COP31, the annual climate negotiations. Countries failed to reach an agreement over fossil fuels - the primary driver of global warming.
text:
Climate change talks fall apart in final hours over fossil fuels
ANTALYA, Turkey — International climate change talks in Antalya, Turkey, broke down in overtime hours over the main cause of planetary warming — fossil fuels. On Sunday, nearly 200 countries failed to reach an agreement on whether they should move away from energy sources like coal and natural gas.
The talks ended in a dramatic fashion, with the European Union negotiators saying they could not agree to a final agreement without mentioning the transition away from fossil fuels — the primary driver of climate change. The EU bloc then walked out of the room. Burning fossil fuels like oil, gas and coal make up roughly 73% of global emissions.
After representatives of the EU walked out, other countries also objected – including Panama and island states such as the Marshall Islands.
The European climate chief, Wopke Hoekstra, said that when the world is heading for an overshoot of 1.5 degrees, the EU could not tolerate an agreement that does not mention fossil fuels. "That is not acceptable," Hoekstra told reporters after walking out of the talks. "We do that with a heavy heart with many other countries, but we simply cannot accept this."
This is the first U.N. climate summit where there's been scientific consensus that the world will surpass a key global warming threshold. Countries agreed in 2015 to limit climate change to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit), but the planet has essentially reached that limit already.
Passing that threshold means more severe climate impacts, like more intense hurricanes and heat waves. The United Nations found that a best-case scenario of 1.7 or 1.8 degrees Celsius would require cutting emissions immediately, reducing them by 45% by 2035. That, scientists say, would require dramatically cutting fossil fuel use.
"It's good that that decision has been rejected," says Mohamed Adow of Power Shift Africa, a nonprofit focused on climate change in Africa. "It doesn't have enough to help protect the people who are most vulnerable to climate change, who have contributed the least and are now suffering firsthand the worst."
NPR correspondent Michael Copley contributed to this story. This story was edited by Sadie Babits.
Correction Nov. 22, 2026
A previous version of this story incorrectly said the European Union walked out along with other countries. In fact, EU representatives walked out while other countries objected.

title: Ghanaian boy killed in US 'deserved so much better', says New York Mayor Mamdani
summary: At the funeral for the 15-year-old who was fatally shot last month, Mamdani spoke alongside the boy's father and civil rights leaders.
text:
Ghanaian boy killed in US 'deserved so much better', says New York Mayor Mamdani
- Published
A 15-year-old Ghanaian boy who was killed in the US last month was remembered as a hard-working student with dreams of becoming a doctor, as his father, New York City's mayor and civil rights leaders gave eulogies during his funeral on Friday.
Javits Frimpong was shot and killed while walking to school in the Bronx. His death has sparked outrage in both Ghana and the US, and reignited debates about gun violence in America.
"Javits deserved so much better and so do every single one of you," Mayor Zohran Mamdani said. "Though he was only a New Yorker for a short time, New York City will forever be proud to call Javits one of our own."
Frimpong moved to the US about a year before the shooting.
"I worked hard to bring you from Ghana to America because I wanted you to have opportunities, a better future, and a chance to achieve everything that you dreamed of," his father, Thomas Frimpong, said.
His mother was granted an emergency visa from Ghana to mourn her son at Friday's funeral service, following Mamdani's lobbying of President Donald Trump earlier this month.
Earlier this month, she told the BBC that she wanted "justice for my son", a sentiment echoed at Friday's service.
Officials have said they are exploring several motives. Frimpong's family has said he experienced bullying at school, which police said they were investigating.
Frimpong was chased down and shot on 29 October. He was taken to a local hospital, where he was pronounced dead.
Police have said three teenage boys were involved in the shooting. A 17-year-old has been arrested and charged with murder, and will be tried as an adult. Police are still searching for the other two.
"Gun violence is never the answer," Ben Crump, an attorney representing the family, said at the funeral as he vowed to seek justice for Frimpong.
Ghana's government has condemned the killing and said it would follow the case closely to ensure justice was achieved.
It has urged US authorities to conduct a thorough investigation and said it was ready to provide legal and consular support to ensure the perpetrators were brought to justice.

title: Three killed and dozens missing after fire at Indonesian factory
summary: At least three people were killed and many more feared dead after a fire at a confectionary factory.
text:
Three killed and dozens missing after fire at Indonesian factory
- Published
At least three people have been killed after a fire at a confectionery factory in western Java on Saturday, with the death toll expected to rise.
Firefighters were still tackling some flames on Sunday, while rescuers searched for around 36 missing in parts of the damaged building where workers were believed to be trapped.
Indonesia's National Search and Rescue Agency said on Sunday 15 survivors had been located, and four others taken to hospital and a local clinic with undisclosed injuries.
Rescuers recovered 24 body bags from the fire as of Sunday evening, as search operations continue to locate missing people.
Banten Governor, Andra Soni, told media about 60 people were believed to be inside the factory when it caught fire on Saturday evening.
The factory is in Serang district, Banten province, about 50km (31km) west of Jakarta. Authorities have not yet determined the fire's cause.
Photos and footage of the scene showed the large factory taken over by flames during the night, firefighters battling the flames, and first responders retrieving at least one body from the wreckage on Sunday morning.
Local media reported that the search had been called off for the night late on Sunday, and would resume on Monday.
"All members of the joint SAR team are making every effort to locate the missing victims while prioritising the safety of personnel on the ground," the rescue agency said.
Relatives of the missing workers had gathered outside the factory waiting for updates, according to local broadcasts cited by AFP.
Firefighters had been called to the building at 16:30 local time (09:30 GMT) on Saturday - but it was already engulfed in flames, broadcaster Kompas TV reported, citing fire official Tubugas Machfudz.
"When we arrived (on location)... a large area was already on fire. So we could not determine whether the company's protection system was functioning properly or not," he said.
The factory is owned by PT Fonusa Agung Mulia, according to search and rescue authorities.
On LinkedIn the company describes itself as a subsidiary of UNIFAM, one of Indonesia's largest food and beverage companies.

title: Medicare looks a bit different in 2027, so don't miss open enrollment
summary: Open enrollment for Medicare runs through Dec. 7, and there are a few different pitfalls people should watch out for this year. Your drug plan or Medicare Advantage plan could be changing a lot.
text:
Medicare looks a bit different in 2027, so don't miss open enrollment
Annual open enrollment is underway for Medicare, the federal program that provides health insurance to roughly 70 million people. The coverage choices are complex and often consequential.
Open enrollment runs through Dec. 7. The plan you choose takes effect on Jan. 1, for the full calendar year.
Build-your-own Medicare menu
Medicare provides health insurance to people 65 or older, as well as to some younger people with disabilities or certain health conditions. But it isn't one plan. It's more like a build-your-own-insurance menu.
Roughly half of beneficiaries are enrolled in traditional Medicare, which consists of Parts A and B. Administered by the federal government, the plan covers hospital stays, skilled nursing care, doctor visits, outpatient care, and preventive screenings. Enrollees can typically see any healthcare provider who accepts Medicare, and they rarely need approval for diagnostic tests, such as MRIs and CT scans. However, there's no cap on out-of-pocket expenses in traditional Medicare, and it doesn't cover most prescriptions or dental, vision, or hearing services.
As a result, most traditional Medicare enrollees buy extra coverage from private insurance companies under Medicare Part D, the prescription drug plan. Some also buy a Medigap policy that covers the costs traditional Medicare leaves behind, such as deductibles, copayments, and coinsurance.
Medicare Advantage
This year, the other half of Medicare beneficiaries opted for privately offered, all-in-one managed-care plans known as Medicare Advantage, usually including prescription drug coverage, dental, and vision. The drawbacks are smaller networks and a greater likelihood that treatments and medications will require prior authorization. Like beneficiaries in traditional Medicare, Medicare Advantage participants also pay Part B premiums.
"People really need to do their research before they enroll in Medicare, because there are trade-offs," said David Lipschutz, a co-director at the Center for Medicare Advocacy.
The hassle saves money
Every fall, insurers that offer Part D and Advantage plans send enrollees a critical document known as an Annual Notice of Change. It's a cheat sheet outlining what will be different in the following year: premiums, deductibles, covered drugs. Consumer advocates and Medicare experts say people sometimes make the costly mistake of throwing it out or filing it away without reading it. Can't find it? Call the insurer and ask for another copy.
The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services projects that the average Part D premium will increase less than $1 a month for a standalone prescription drug plan, describing the market as stable. title: US declassifies more UFO footage filmed in the Middle East
summary: The Pentagon has released an eighth tranche of UFO records, which includes three video clips recorded in 2020, 2023 and 2026.
text:
US declassifies more UFO footage filmed in the Middle East
The US government released an eighth tranche of records regarding Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena (UAPs), marking the latest step in an effort to declassify government files on UFOs.
After US President Donald Trump called for UFO files to be released in an executive order earlier this year, the Pentagon has declassified hundreds of files. The first tranche was released 8 May 2026.
The footage in this video makes up three of the 43 files released in this tranche. All three clips were filmed from aboard US military platforms in the Middle East in 2020, 2023 and 2026.

title: South Korea education minister resigns over exam cheating scandal
summary: Choi Kyo-jin admits last-minute measures to stop AI-assisted cheating during the college entrance exam caused chaos.
text:
South Korea education minister resigns over exam cheating scandal
- Published
South Korea's Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin has resigned over an exam cheating scandal that shocked the nation.
He said he took full responsibility for the confusion caused by last-minute measures aimed at stopping AI-assisted cheating during Thursday's annual college entrance exam, known as Suneung.
A week ago, the top scorer in the national tax accountancy exam admitted using a mini-camera, mobile phone and AI tools. This prompted officials to act urgently to detect hidden devices, including sending emergency alerts to every single mobile phone in the country.
The Suneung takes up to nine hours to complete, and it plays a big role in career trajectories of millions of South Koreans.
"As the minister in charge, I believe I cannot escape criticism that we failed to prepare in advance," Choi was quoted as saying on Sunday by South Korea's Yonhap's news agency.
"Now that the exam has concluded, I feel a deep sense of responsibility and am offering my resignation," the minister added.
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung - who has been calling for an overhaul of the current exam system - later accepted Choi's resignation.
The education ministry earlier said 111 candidates had been found with unauthorised smart devices during this year's Suneung, which was taken by about 500,000 students.
Concerns over academic dishonesty during the fiercely competitive exam had been brewing in recent weeks, after reports of candidates cheating with the help of AI devices.
These fears came to a boil last weekend, when Han Won-seok, the top tax accountancy exam scorer in April, admitted to cheating.
His confession came amid speculation over his unusually high score, with just one out of 160 questions wrong.
"I used a microcamera to photograph the test questions and sent them to an AI, then checked my answers on my smartphone to commit the cheating," the 34-year-old said in a video message.
This prompted the authorities to introduce urgent measures, with just days ahead of the Suneung.
This included sending nationwide emergency alerts on the exam day.
Three alerts were sent between 08:00 and 15:00 local time on Thursday, causing phones across the country to blare out in unison - even if they were on silent mode, and even if they belonged to tourists using data roaming.
The phones did not ring out if they were switched off or on airplane mode.
It was the first time that South Korea used its national disaster alert system to catch exam cheaters.
Candidates also had to cover up the buttons on their shirts and jackets to block any hidden cameras, and authorities conducted inspections of eyewear.
All this made even honest test takers paranoid.

title: NPR's Senior Podcast Challenge: Early entries we love
summary: People 65 and older have been submitting stories for a chance to win our grand prize — a visit to NPR watch your podcast air live on Weekend Edition . There's still time to enter!
text:
NPR's Senior Podcast Challenge: Early entries we love
Once people hit retirement age, there are so many questions: Who am I without my job? What do I do to fill this time? How are my relationships changing?
This fall, for the first-ever NPR Senior Podcast Challenge, we asked those of you in the over-65 crowd, to tell us about all this, and you've been sending in your answers.
The competition flips the story line on our popular NPR Student Podcast Challenge – since 2018 more than 90,000 young people have sent us their stories, in their own voices.
Now, we're hearing from listeners with a lot of experience, hopefully some wisdom, and perhaps more grey hair.
While the contest is still open for a few more weeks — you have until November 30 to enter — we've been listening to more than 100 podcasts that have come in so far.
Here's a sample of some of our early favorites:
Lou Ann Baylock, of Sarasota, Fla., told us she wasn't too happy about the title of our contest: the "senior" part.
"I'm 68, but I'm NOT a senior, am I?" she asks in her podcast, Talk to Me.
"I thought seniors were people in their 80s," she says. "I mean, I see my body changing. I know I'm getting older. But am I really a senior?"
Baylock ends up deciding she's OK with that term: She's still working, and as a therapist she tells us in her podcast she has some ideas that might help other people her age.
Finding the joy
Many of our podcasters took up the issue of life after retirement. Some of you are telling us you're having the best time of your life. Others, not so much.
For Martin Goldsmith, 78, of Tacoma, Wash., retirement means not letting his age keep him doing the things he loves.
"The back, the legs, and the joints aren't what they used to be," he says in his entry Joy Filled Retirement. "So for me, the running and skiing are out and the hearing aids are in."
But, he adds, "I can still play my guitar."
Music, Goldsmith tells us, has always been in his DNA. He grew up jamming with his dad on the clarinet and mom on the viola. And he's now playing his guitar at the children's hospital, and he ends his story playing and singing an old favorite, Nobody Knows You When You're Down and Out.
Putting yourself out there
And then, there's dating. We've received quite a few podcasts about life post-divorce, or after losing a partner.
Our podcasters are reminding us that it never gets easier, and many of them including George Smith have told us some version of this: "I never thought I'd be here."
Smith lives with his daughter in Wildomar, Calif., and when it came to figuring out the modern dating scene, he says:
"After almost three decades of marriage, I found myself in my mid-60s, divorced, alone in a cafe, and about to meet a woman from a dating app for the first time in my life. Little did I realize," he tells us, "my teenage daughter Shannon would become my dating navigator."
Smith's podcast is aptly called Swipe Right, Dad, and he tells us about three very different online dates he goes

title: Birds killed in blaze at one of the largest foie gras farms in the US
summary: Hundreds of young birds were also rescued from the fire, which comes as foie gras is under renewed scrutiny over animal welfare concerns.
text:
Birds killed in blaze at one of the largest foie gras farms in the US
- Published
A fire broke out at one of the largest foie gras farms in the US on Thursday, killing an undetermined number of birds.
The blaze engulfed several barns at Hudson Valley Farms in upstate New York before firefighters could get inside. No information has been provided as to what caused the fire.
Crews managed to rescue hundreds of young birds and hatchlings, and no workers or first responders were injured, according to local news outlets.
Foie gras, made from the fattened liver of a duck or goose, has long drawn protests from animal rights groups because the birds are force-fed. Voters in both Washington DC and Denver backed bans on foie gras sales in this month's midterm elections.
Marcus Henley, manager of Hudson Valley Foie Gras in Ferndale, New York, told local news outlet Radio Catskill that the fire destroyed two buildings housing ducks and geese.
"The building isn't there anymore," Henley said, adding that he suspected an electrical malfunction may have started the blaze, although this has not been confirmed.
The company does not disclose how many birds it hosts at one time. Commercial poultry farms can typically house thousands of birds.
Westchester News 12 reported that the emergency response to the fire in the early hours of Thursday morning involved 37 fire departments and 200 first responders.
The fire spread rapidly, and the metal-clad, wood-frame structure of the building made it difficult for firefighters to stop the flames from spreading inside the barn.
Hudson Valley Foie Gras and the local fire department did not respond to a request for comment.
Foie gras producers have long been criticised by animal rights groups due to the production process, which involves the force feeding of birds through plastic tubes, which allows them to gain over a third of their body weight in a short period of time.
New York moved to ban the product in 2019, and Hudson Valley farms have been in litigation with the state since.
At a city council hearing in 2019, Henley argued against the ban, saying that journalists who visited the farm found "nothing inhumane" about their practices.
Animal rights activist group PETA told the BBC that they will erect a billboard nearby in memory of the birds who perished, and encouraged Hudson Valley farms to donate surviving birds to local sanctuaries.

title: Italian jeweller and businessman Paolo Bulgari dies aged 89
summary: In a statement to Italian media, his family remember him as "the greatest jeweller of our time".
text:
Italian jeweller and businessman Paolo Bulgari dies aged 89
- Published
Italian jeweller Paolo Bulgari, who helped turn his family's business into a global luxury brand, has died in Rome aged age 89.
His family announced the news, remembering him as "the greatest jeweller of our time", according to Italian media.
Paolo Bulgari was Chairman of the Bvlgari Group since 1984 and its jewellery pieces have adorned Hollywood stars and royalty including Diana, Princess of Wales.
The company Bvlgari posted an online tribute to the "true creative soul", whose work would "continue to inspire generations to come".
The firm, Bulgari, was set up by his grandfather, Greek silversmith Sotirios Voulgaris, in Rome in the late 19th century - who later adapted his name to Bulgari in Italian.
Originally from Paramythia, a mountain village in the Epirus region of northwestern Greece renowned for its silver jewellery, Voulgaris fled Ottoman rule and settled in Naples before opening a shop in Rome.
Paolo Bulgari joined the company shortly after leaving school, becoming an expert in gemstones - eventually leading the business and overseeing international growth.
The Bulgari family favoured bold gemstones, rich yellow gold, generous proportions and unexpected colour combinations to set them apart from the delicate asethetic associated with Parisian jewellery houses.
The business broke into luxury markets and diversified beyond jewellery into watches, perfumes, leather goods and hotels.
"Paolo Bulgari began collaborating with his father in 1960, specialising in the knowledge of precious stones, of which he was one of the world's leading experts, and refining the sensibility and aesthetic sense that are at the root of the Bvlgari style," the Bvlgari company posted on social media., external
"He poured his heart into his craft and into nurturing the talents of young designers, leaving an indelible mark on the world of jewellery.
"Thank you, Mr. Paolo, your legacy as a brilliant beacon of creative inspiration will continue to inspire generations to come."
The post included a quote from Paolo Bulgari: "Everything can be a source of inspiration. There are no rules in creativity. Never."
The designer brand's celebrity clients have included Elizabeth Taylor, Audrey Hepburn, Marilyn Monroe, Ingrid Bergman, Sophie Loren, Anne Hathaway, Zendaya and Rihanna.
In 2011 the family sold its controlling stake to the French luxury group LVMH, in a deal worth about 3.7 billion euros.
In 2019, he and his wife established the Paolo Bulgari Foundation to support young people through schooling and job training in disadvantaged neighbourhoods on the outskirts of Rome.
The funeral will take place in Rome on Monday, 23 November in the Basilica of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme.
  - Published7 March 2011

title: He expected a small-business loan. He got a 7-year nightmare
summary: America's fastest-growing source of funding for small businesses is also one of the least regulated. One man has waged a long, lonely fight to recoup its punishing cost.
text:
He expected a small-business loan. He got a 7-year nightmare
GLENDALE, Calif. — Sitting at his desk, tucked into a corner of his teenage bedroom — a place where he'd never intended to return, well into middle age — Vahe Shahinian rereads the emails that split his life into before and after.
A broker was offering to fund Shahinian's small business with a line of credit worth $750,000.
It was 2019, and Shahinian's company soared, like a miniature Live Nation-Ticketmaster, selling tickets and producing concerts around Los Angeles and beyond. He imagined how much he could do with stable funding.
The pitch had a catch: Shahinian would first accept a third of the sum and start paying it back immediately, in daily installments of $3,600. After 30 days, he could access the rest of the money. He crunched the numbers, followed up with questions — and took the deal.
Shahinian sent the daily payments, he says, for 30 days. Then 40. Then 50.
The line of credit never came.
"From that day," he says, "it's been one long day, one long nightmare."
For seven years, Shahinian has been mired in the shadowy industry that is now the fastest-growing source of funding for small business in the United States. It's largely unregulated, promising fast money at a tremendous cost. And Shahinian's lawsuit against his funders could become one of the first of its kind to go to trial.
A business in need
Before the "incident," as Shahinian calls his fateful deal, he'd been in business for 15 years, building his company from a side hustle into his main source of income.
Educated as a computer scientist, he'd spent years programming satellites as an aerospace engineer. In 2004, he also developed a site for something he loved in his spare time: community events. Shahinian called his platform for ticketing and seating charts It's My Seat.
Over a decade, Shahinian grew his business from selling tickets to galas and festivals to producing his own shows: booking artists and venues, promoting and marketing. His first concert, by a flamenco guitarist, sold 400 seats. The next, 700. Three years later, 1960s crooner Engelbert Humperdinck performed for 3,000. In 2015, Shahinian expanded again, into touring.
Like most U.S. small businesses, Shahinian says, he self-funded for years. Entrepreneurs like him often dip into savings, family money or home equity; many run up credit cards and reinvest profits.
Shahinian says he had qualified for several generous credit cards, including an American Express with essentially no spending limit. Later, Amex also repeatedly approved him for special merchant financing: instant short-term loans with a low interest rate of 6%.
"All my life," Shahinian offers as his frequent disclaimer these days, "I had never had one missed payment."
By 2018, Shahinian says, he had built his retirement plan: His ticket sales climbed toward $5 million a year, his profits $250,000.

title: Tech stock sell-off drags markets down as Anthropic shares slide
summary: Pressures weighed on US markets, with the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average pushed into correction territory.
text:
Tech stock sell-off drags markets down as Anthropic shares slide
- Published
Anthropic's shares have dropped back towards their initial price after a soaring first day on the stock market, as a wider tech sell-off dragged markets down.
The sell-off comes as concerns remain over the speed and size of artificial intelligence investment, but also as some large companies including Nvidia and SpaceX faced specific issues that worried investors.
Those pressures combined to weigh on US markets through Friday, with all key US indexes closing sharply down on the day, furthering earlier falls over the week.
Both the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average were pushed into correction territory, a point where they are trading at 10% or more down from a recent high.
The S&P 500 closed down 3.7%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 1.9% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index plunged 5.3%. However, all three indexes were up on where they were a year ago.
The speed at which AI investment has been growing - with more than $1 trillion spent in the last year alone by a small handful of major tech companies - has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble. Questions are being raised over whether those investments will pay off, and when.
Investors were also spooked after the Democrats' resounding win in the US midterms in early November, which sparked fears of a reduction in AI development.
Despite a positive first day of trading, Anthropic's shares fell on Friday, dropping at one point by more than 12% to about $85, close to its initial public offering (IPO) price of $83. It closed down 8.5%, reversing half of the gains made on Thursday.
The artificial intelligence (AI) company's introduction to the Nasdaq stock exchange on Thursday was a crucial test for the industry and was largely seen as a success, with trading starting at $111.50 before easing to end the day up 17% at $97.17.
Analysts said volatility was to be expected in the first days or even weeks of Anthropic's trading, as the company was the first frontier AI firm to go public so had no direct peers.
Some have also noted the similarities with Elon Musk's SpaceX, which at the time of its debut in June was the largest IPO on record. Shares in the rocket and AI company experienced large swings in its first few weeks of trading.
Ed Moya, a strategist at market intelligence firm AlphaSense, said Anthropic's blockbuster IPO did not appear to have restored confidence in the broader AI market.
While AI demand was still very strong, Moya told the BBC that investors were trying to answer the question of how much were they willing to pay for that growth.
"As we've gone through the past past few weeks, it seems that there's been more risks that have surfaced," he said.
"Right now you're starting to see Wall Street is trying to shift from rewarding growth at any price, to demanding stronger cash flow and a clearer path to profitability."

title: Nigerian youth have shown their power in the past - why aren't they shaping this election?
summary: Fewer young people have registered to vote in next year's election than in 2023 - are young people losing faith in democracy?
text:
Nigerian youth have shown their power in the past - why aren't they shaping this election?
- Published
Abdulhadi Dalhatu is something of a rarity in Nigeria politics.
At 38, he is among the young people seeking elected office in a country where about 80% of the population is under 40.
He hopes his age will stand in his favour as he campaigns for a seat in the state assembly in the northern Kano state in January's general elections.
"Younger people are the majority in this country and should be deciding the future," Dalhatu tells the BBC.
But Nigeria's political history suggests he faces an uphill battle.
Since the return to civilian rule in 1999, Goodluck Jonathan has been the youngest person elected president, taking office at the age of 53.
The current president, Bola Tinubu, is 74 and would be 79 by the end of a second term if he is re-elected in January.
His main challengers are also considerably older. Atiku Abubakar, seeking the presidency for the seventh time, is 79, while Peter Obi is 65.
Of the 18 presidential candidates, only one is under 40 - Moses Olusoji Adebisi, a 35-year-old businessman representing the Democratic Leadership Alliance (DLA).
Although he says he is confident of winning, few Nigerians appear to know much about him and he has not been seen much on the campaign trail.
The contrast is striking in a country with one of the world's youngest populations, where young people have repeatedly demonstrated their ability to shape political debate and mobilise for change.
In the previous election, Obi, then 61, galvanised millions of young Nigerians through a social media-driven movement known as the "Obedients".
His campaign promised a break from the established political order, appealing particularly to young people struggling to find jobs and earn a decent living.
But his failure to win the presidency left many of his supporters disillusioned.
"At the time we were so hopeful, but unfortunately the result wasn't what we wanted, which made many lose hope in the system," former Obedient Nonso Chukwudi tells the BBC.
The movement had built on the momentum of the EndSars protests in 2020, which grew into one of Nigeria's biggest youth-led movement in decades.
Initially sparked by anger over police brutality, the demonstrators developed into a wider call for political reform, accountability and greater youth participation in governance.
But the protests were eventually crushed by the authorities. About 56 were reportedly killed, although officials dispute this figure, while hundreds were arrested and some had their bank accounts frozen.
Both EndSars and the Obedients demonstrated the capacity of young Nigerians to mobilise around political causes.
But turning that enthusiasm into sustained electoral participation has proved much harder.
Hajara Musa, 33, is among those who have lost faith in the political system. She has no plans to register or vote in the near future.

title: Trump orders federal contractors to check with White House before responding to Congress
summary: President Trump is directing federal contractors to consult the White House about inquiries from Congress and to withhold any communications that his administration considers privileged.
text:
Trump orders federal contractors to check with White House before responding to Congress
NEW YORK (AP) — President Donald Trump is directing federal contractors and subcontractors to consult with his administration about inquiries they receive from Congress and to withhold any communications that the White House considers privileged, according to a new executive order.
The companies must also coordinate with the White House and U.S. agencies on "appropriate responses" to any such requests, the order issued late Friday says. If they fail to comply, the White House warns their contracts could be terminated and their future work with the federal government suspended.
The order is the Republican administration's latest effort to resist what are expected to be wide-ranging and aggressive oversight efforts from Democrats when they take over Congress in January. Democrats have made government contracts one of their top investigative targets, noting that federal money has been flowing to companies linked with Trump's family, particularly at the Pentagon.
White House officials have already begun taking steps to exert more control over how agencies and officials respond to congressional requests, anticipating there will be a flood of investigations initiated by Democrats.
Trump's counsel, Will Scharf, told federal agencies on Monday that they must seek approval from his office and the White House's Office of Legislative Affairs before agreeing to appear before Congress. Scharf also suggested in a recent letter to Rep. Robert Garcia of California, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, that some congressional investigations may amount to "blatant criminality."
Garcia sent letters this week directing members of Trump's family and top administration officials to preserve documents. Scharf sought to dismiss the requests, noting in a letter to Democratic lawmakers that they are not yet in the majority and cannot compel compliance.
Responding to the new executive order, Garcia said it was part of the administration's "blatant attack on Congress' constitutional right to conduct oversight." He said that despite efforts to impede investigations, "we're just getting started."
In a fact sheet, the White House framed the new requirements as "protecting executive privileges from congressional overreach," arguing that some congressional leaders have tried to intrude on executive branch privileges by "harassing private companies that contract with the federal government."
Presidents of both parties have long used executive privilege to resist congressional inquiries, but the claims can set up messy, protracted legal fights as parties dispute whether it applies. Executive privilege allows the president to keep information from the courts, Congress and the public to protect the confidentiality of White House deliberations, but the protection is far from absolute.

title: Removal of hat inside Fiona the hippo was 'impossible', Cincinnati Zoo says
summary: The location of the hat and the 2,400-pound animal's anatomy made removal unfeasible, the zoo said.
text:
Removal of hat inside Fiona the hippo was 'impossible', Cincinnati Zoo says
- Published
The hat swallowed by beloved hippopotamus Fiona had become lodged in the middle of her small intestine, making removal "impossible", the Cincinnati Zoo in Ohio said.
Vets tried to save Fiona after she ingested the hat that ended up in her habitat by accident almost two weeks ago. But its location and the 2,400-pound (1,088 kg) animal's anatomy made removal unfeasible. She died on Thursday.
A necropsy, an autopsy performed on an animal, showed the hat was "located 25 feet beyond the final stomach compartment and 50 feet from the end of her intestines", the zoo said on Friday.
Animal lovers were rooting for a recovery for Fiona, who became a social media star after her premature birth in 2017.
Cincinnati Zoo's director of animal health, Dr Mike Wenninger, said in a statement that an upper and lower GI endoscopy were unable to reach the object.
"The location and anatomy made laparoscopic removal impossible," Wenninger added. "No treatment aside from supportive care had any chance for success, and the necropsy confirmed that no amount of supportive care would have worked."
Michelle Curley, a spokesperson for the zoo, had said that the woollen hat got into Fiona's enclosure by accident, after a visitor tossed it in the air and it caught on a ceiling fan that flung it through a small opening.
"We probably couldn't make [it] happen again if we tried," Curley said.
While Fiona showed no symptoms at first, her appetite started to decrease a few days later, and the zoo staff tried to encourage Fiona to eat to help push the hat through her digestive system to no avail.
Christina Gorsuch, The zoo's director of animal care, Christina Gorsuch, said on Friday that the other hippos - Bibi, Tucker and Fritz - were so far eating and behaving normally after Fiona's passing.
"It's difficult to know how they're feeling, but they appear to be their normal selves, Gorsuch said.
"We have received so much love from our community and beyond," said Cincinnati Zoo director Dave Jenike. "We were touched when we saw stadiums, bridges, and buildings lit in purple last night" in Fiona's [honour], he added.
The US Senate even adopted a resolution on Friday to honour the beloved hippo.
Fiona first rose to fame when she was born premature at Cincinnati Zoo in 2017 and at first struggled to survive. At birth, she weighed 13 kg (29 lbs), which the zoo said was about half the previous lowest recorded birth weight for her species.
"The support that we're feeling from all over the world reminds me of the time when everyone pulled together to root for her to survive," Jenike said. "She did, and she gave us almost a decade of smiles."

title: How a teen gamer and his mother helped rescue a missing girl
summary: When 16-year-old Landon Tresp met a teenage girl in an online game, it led to him and his mother helping the FBI rescue her from kidnapping.
text:
How a teen gamer and his mother helped rescue a missing girl
- Published
Sixteen-year-old Landon Tresp was in the bedroom of his family's Colorado mountain home, playing an online game after finishing his daily chores, when he began chatting on his laptop with another player.
She was also a teenager, and the pair "kind of just clicked," he tells the BBC.
He told her he liked her name, and she confessed that it was an alias. She was a runaway, she said - and was being held against her will, hundreds of miles from home, though she didn't know exactly where. The girl, 17, and had been missing for more than a year.
Stunned, Landon felt "helpless," he says - and, after learning more details over two weeks of chatting, he decided to tell his mother, Khristina on 31 October this year. The 41-year-old nurse and mother of five was putting Halloween makeup on her younger children for trick-or-treating when he briefed her.
That set the mother and son on a path to track down his friend, contact her mother, cooperate with the FBI - and ultimately witness the rescue of the teen - only 24 hours after Landon first alerted Khristina to her plight.
"She had one opportunity to reach out her hand and ask for help, and she chose me," Khristina says of the girl, who was 15 when she went missing.
The Tresps have shared with BBC screenshots of communication with the girl and a photo matching the criminal complaint to corroborate their story.
Landon first told his mother about "Jenny" - whose identity the BBC is protecting - in mid-October, a few weeks before the rescue.
"He had mentioned something about maybe a week or so into talking to her that he met a girl online, and she was really sweet," says Khristina - who cautioned him that "you don't always know who's on the other side of the screen".
"She's just having a really hard time and looking for a friend," he told her.
But Landon was becoming increasingly concerned as Jenny told him more about her situation.
They'd met playing Among Us, a game Landon describes as "kind of like online space Clue".
After telling Landon that she was a runaway, "Jenny" said an older man had taken her across state lines and wouldn't let her leave. She was the subject of a missing person investigation, and she sent Landon links to stories about her disappearance. But she believed police were no longer looking for her.
Jenny was scared and desperate, and that's why Landon went to his mother.
Her maternal instincts on high alert, Khristina contacted Jenny herself on Discord, the encrypted platform.
During the conversation, Khristina said she told the Colorado mother how she'd been through "years of abuse in her life and lots and lots of problems".
Within hours, Jenny started calling Khristina "mama".
The Colorado mother knew things were serious when she read the missing persons articles. Jenny knew she was in Oregon and gave the name of a city, but she didn't know where she was being held exactly. Khristina knew she needed more. She told Jen

title: Google employees protest AI in schools policy
summary: More than 550 Google employees signed a petition to allow schools access to Search without AI. Parents and educators protested outside Google offices in 6 cities last week for the same ask.
text:
Google employees protest AI in schools policy
More than 550 Google employees signed a petition to allow schools access to Search without AI. Parents and educators protested outside Google offices in 6 cities last week for the same ask.
ROB SCHMITZ, HOST:
Parents and educators want Google to provide an AI-free version of the search engine for students. The backlash started after the company announced that they would not unbundle AI from their tools for education. Now some Google employees are joining in the push to provide AI-free access to students. NPR education reporter Sequoia Carrillo is following the story. She joins us now. Hey, Sequoia.
SEQUOIA CARRILLO, BYLINE: Hi.
SCHMITZ: So parents have mixed feelings, obviously, about using AI in the classroom. Why is Google taking such a firm stance on this?
CARRILLO: I think mixed feelings is actually kind of a nice read of the situation. I've pretty much only talked to very angry parents, and we have a lot of very angry legislators, too, at the state and at national levels. Why Google's taking such a firm stance? There's no clear answer. I mean, some will point you to the fact that Google's very heavily invested in AI, and they want schools to be just as invested in it.
And I actually spoke to some people who pointed me towards two court cases earlier this year. Google got those dismissed by arguing that AI Overview and their search function are one tool. And those dismissals might mean that breaking them up could potentially be legally difficult for them. And when I talk to Google, they would not give us comments. So who is to say right now?
SCHMITZ: That's really interesting. So it sounds like Google has sort of backed itself into a legal corner on this issue, and it sounds like Google's own employees are angry about this.
CARRILLO: Yes. So Google employees are now weighing in. A small percentage signed a petition to allow schools the option to use search without AI overview, and the union for Google employees says that they're worried that this could damage the company's reputation among students and teachers and end up with schools ultimately shutting out Google's products altogether. There is some merit to that. Earlier this month, we saw protests across the country outside of Google offices because of this exact stance.
SCHMITZ: So what are schools doing to prepare for this change?
CARRILLO: People are definitely finding workarounds, and if they haven't already found it, they're definitely working on it. They say something as simple as the Chrome extension might be able to help districts keep the search engine. Fairfax County, a very large, well-funded district in Northern Virginia, was actually already doing this. They're piloting a kind of ad-blocking-type tool for AI on their school devices that they developed.
SCHMITZ: OK. So if one school district in Virginia can do this, why is this an issue? Why doesn't everyone do this?
